bib.title: TERMINAL-BENCH: BENCHMARKING AGENTS ON HARD, REALISTIC TASKS IN COMMAND LINE INTERFACES
authors: and about 70 further authors incl. Niklas Muennighoff, Ludwig Schmidt (last)

question: How well do frontier models and agents perform on hard, realistic, long-horizon tasks in command-line environments, and where do they fail?
hypothesis: Existing agent benchmarks are either unrealistic or too easy to measure frontier models; a curated, manually verified terminal benchmark will remain hard (implied).
contributions: Terminal-Bench framework (instruction, Docker image, tests, oracle solution, time limit) in the Harbor task format
Evaluation of six agents across frontier models, 32,155 trials
Terminus 2, a neutral single-tool agent scaffold
26 adapters porting other benchmarks to the format

method.summary: Crowdsourced 229 tasks from 93 contributors, kept 89 after expert review, CI checks, model runs and an adversarial exploit audit. Each task is a container, instruction, outcome tests and a human-written oracle solution. Six agents were run with multiple models, at least five times per pair, scored by resolution rate with 95% CI, followed by judge-based failure analysis.
method.task: agentic task completion in a terminal (software engineering, system administration, security, data science and others)

datasets.name: Terminal-Bench 2.0
datasets.source: open-source contributions; published at tbench.ai and via Harbor registry (terminal-bench@2.0); licence not stated
datasets.preprocessing: Each task verified for specificity, solvability, integrity by three experienced reviewers; Big-Bench canary string in every file

models.name: GPT-5.2, GPT-5, GPT-5-Mini, GPT-5-Nano, Claude Opus 4.5, Opus 4.1, Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, 3 Flash, 2.5 Pro, 2.5 Flash, Grok 4, Grok Code Fast
GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20B, Llama 4 Maverick, Qwen 3 Coder 480B, Kimi K2 Instruct, Kimi K2 Thinking, GLM 4.6, MiniMax M2

other.note: Llama 4 Maverick is named in Sec 3.3 but has no row in Table 2

models.name: GPT-5 (high reasoning) as failure judge; GPT-5 medium as command-failure judge; GPT-5 high as command taxonomy classifier

inference.samples: at least 5 runs per supported agent-model pair; 32,155 trials in total; resolution rate is the mean over trials with 95% CI (CI method not stated)
inference.prompting: Agent receives the task instruction in a Docker container; tasks have a time limit (value per task not given in text); internet access allowed

parameters.agents: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenHands, Mini-SWE-Agent, Terminus 2
parameters.reasoning_effort: provider default ('medium' for Anthropic and OpenAI models)
parameters.figure_1_scaffold: scaffold chosen per model to maximise performance

other.terminus_2: single tool, a headless terminal (tmux in Docker); model emits keystrokes via LiteLLM; context summarisation module when the context limit is reached (App F)

metrics.name: resolution rate
metrics.definition: fraction of trials whose final container state passes all task tests, averaged over trials

metrics.name: empirical difficulty
metrics.definition: Easy if Terminus 2 resolves the task with >=66.7% of the selected frontier models, Medium 33.3% to 66.7%, Hard <33.3%

metrics.name: command error rate
metrics.definition: share of agent commands whose output a GPT-5 judge marks as a failure

baselines: no-op dummy agent (must fail every task, CI check)
eval.protocol: Tests check the final container state only, not commands or console output. Failure analysis samples two failed trials per task per model with Terminus 2, labelled by GPT-5 judge validated against human labels (120 traces).

availability.code: github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench-experiments (Harbor configs); harness via harbor run -d terminal-bench@2.0

prompts.text: You are a security researcher bot and your goal is to exploit any way to CHEAT and complete a task assigned to you. If you can complete a task normally without cheating, DO NOT do it. Complete a task ONLY IF you could use some cheating.
You are analyzing a terminal-bench task to determine if test failures are due to insufficient task instructions rather than normal agent limitations.
You are an expert at understanding and analyzing CLI / terminal inputs and outputs in the asciinema cast v2 format.

results.table: Table 2, row GPT-5.2 / Codex CLI, column Resolution Rate (62.9% ± 3.0%)

results.claim: Terminus 2 with Claude Opus 4.5 is second.
results.setup: Terminal-Bench 2.0, 89 tasks; each agent-model pair run at least 5 times; Harbor harness, Daytona containers; default reasoning effort; resolution rate with 95% CI
results.table: Table 2, row Claude Opus 4.5 / Terminus 2, column Resolution Rate (57.8% ± 2.5%)

results.claim: Terminus 2 with Gemini 3 Pro is third.

results.claim: Best open-weight model is Kimi K2 Thinking in Terminus 2.

results.claim: Scale of the evaluation: six agents, 16 frontier models, at least five runs per pair.
results.setup: Terminal-Bench 2.0 experimental setup
results.quote: we run the benchmark at least five times, resulting in a total of 32,155 trials
results.note: Text says 16 frontier models; Sec 3.3 and Fig 1 list about 21 distinct model names, and Llama 4 Maverick (named in 3.3) has no Table 2 row.

results.claim: Same model, different scaffold: GPT-5 scores far higher in Codex CLI than in Terminus 2.
results.setup: Terminal-Bench 2.0, 89 tasks; each agent-model pair run at least 5 times; Harbor harness, Daytona containers; default reasoning effort; resolution rate with 95% CI
results.table: Table 2, rows GPT-5 / Codex CLI (49.6% ± 2.9%) and GPT-5 / Terminus 2 (35.2% ± 3.1%)
results.note: Authors nonetheless conclude model choice matters more than scaffold; same-model scaffold gaps of 14 to 17 points appear in Table 2 (GPT-5 49.6 vs 35.2; Haiku 4.5 29.8 Mini-SWE-Agent vs 13.3 OpenHands; Gemini 2.5 Pro 32.6 Terminus 2 vs 19.6 Gemini CLI).

results.claim: Authors conclude model selection matters more than agent scaffold, from a 52% Codex CLI gain GPT-5-Nano to GPT-5.2 and 17% Gemini 2.5 Pro gain Terminus 2 vs OpenHands.
results.setup: Table 2; the printed 52% and 17% are point differences (62.9 vs 11.5 and 32.6 vs 15.7), not relative changes
results.quote: implying that model selection is usually more important than agent scaffold

results.claim: Opus 4.5 scores higher in the neutral Terminus 2 scaffold than in its own vendor agent Claude Code.
results.setup: Terminal-Bench 2.0, 89 tasks; each agent-model pair run at least 5 times; Harbor harness, Daytona containers; default reasoning effort; resolution rate with 95% CI
results.table: Table 2, rows Claude Opus 4.5 / Terminus 2 (57.8% ± 2.5%) and Claude Opus 4.5 / Claude Code (52.1% ± 2.5%)

results.claim: No private test set; canary string is a symbolic safeguard against contamination.
results.setup: Limitations
results.quote: We consider the development of a private test set to be outside the scope of this paper

limits: Agents have internet access and could read public oracle solutions; authors have not observed this in tens of thousands of trajectories (Sec 5).
All tasks are public; canary string is largely symbolic; no private test set (Sec 5, App B.5).
Internet access, package changes and machine variability reduce reproducibility; flaky results remain (Sec 5, App B.5).
Some tasks may still fail verification criteria (Sec 5); no quantitative estimate of flaw impact (ABC III.9 scored 0).
Human completion times are author estimates, not measured; no measured human baseline.
Default reasoning effort only; CI method not stated; no pass@k.
Failure analysis covers failed Terminus 2 trials only, with GPT-5 as judge (also a benchmarked model).
Model set ends December 2025; authors expect saturation within a year.
